spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The working device is an entire localizer built by averaging a rescaled Fourier-Laplace kernel across an interval. It has nearly unit modulus in the interior, rapid decay beyond an enlarged interval, controlled growth just off the boundary line, and decay in the real direction, so a hard rectangle is replaced by an analytic weight compatible with strip arguments.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Starting from a smooth compactly supported V with V(1)=1, the source defines δη as an entire transform, proves rapid decay away from its center by integration by parts, and sets η=L/Δ in an oscillatory integral ΦΔ,L over [-L,L]. Fourier inversion gives interior approximation, while the transform bound gives exterior decay and uniform decay as the real part tends to infinity.
directed.conceptual_reading: Smoothing makes geometric localization analytically movable: the rectangle indicator is not preserved pointwise, but its useful interior/exterior distinction survives with quantified transition and off-axis errors.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge is from a compactly supported smooth frequency profile V to an entire test function ΦΔ,L that can enter a vertical-strip norm while still behaving like an interval cutoff in the imaginary coordinate.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The localizer is only approximate; it has boundary margins, and its error grows with horizontal displacement according to the Δ/L scaling. The span does not justify treating it as an exact indicator or extending the stated bounds outside their parameter ranges.
directed.uncertainty: The mechanism is clear, but the extracted PDF damages fractions and inequality symbols. Exact half-plane boundaries, constants, and displayed error powers require scan verification.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: A weighted integral over the whole real line is the intermediary that lets strip convexity move a short zeta moment from an off-axis line to the critical boundary. The weight is then removed by being near one on the target window and by killing a dyadic-style family of exterior annuli on one high-probability maximum event.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The proof first replaces ζ by a finite Dirichlet approximation D, defines I(σ) as the integral of |D|^β against |ΦΔ,L|^β, and applies the preceding analytic localizer with Gabriel-type convexity to compare I(σ) to the boundary-line integral. With Δ=log^ε T and L proportional to log^θ T, the central window is unsmoothed from below; outside a threefold window, annuli U_l are bounded using a uniform event S(T) and rapid decay of Φ, making their total negligible.
directed.conceptual_reading: The argument separates transport from truncation: analyticity transports a smoothed norm across the strip, while probabilistic maximum control pays for removing the smoothing. Neither part alone yields the short-interval comparison.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The entire localizer converts a finite-interval moment into a global analytic norm; the annular decomposition converts the global tail back into summable local maximum estimates.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The conclusion is a high-probability inequality in a restricted off-axis range and depends on the Dirichlet approximation, the strip comparison, and the event S(T). It is not a pointwise comparison of ζ values and does not make failed proof search or a bad event mathematically impossible.
directed.uncertainty: The reduction order is explicit, but extraction corrupts the precise σ range, interval factors, and several negligible log powers; those quantitative details need the PDF scan.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The mollifier is a finite Möbius-weighted inverse whose allowed number of prime factors grows with the interval parameter. A strong pointwise mean-square error is deliberately over-budgeted so discretization and Markov can promote inversion at one shift to uniform inversion over the whole growing interval.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The source defines M(s) by summing μ(n)n^{-s} over integers with primes at most X and Ω(n) at most νθ, evaluates slightly off the critical line at σ0, and aims to show max over |h|≤log^θ T of |ζM-1| is small with probability tending to one. For θ>0 it strengthens the L2 estimate by choosing νθ proportional to e^θ log log T, controls the Euler-product and omitted-prime remainders, and then combines Dirichlet-polynomial length bounds, Proposition 2.7, and Markov's inequality. For θ≤0 the earlier fixed-interval proof suffices.
directed.conceptual_reading: Uniformity is bought through slack: the inverse is truncated more generously so its average error is far smaller than needed at one point, leaving enough decay to pay for the number of locations inspected.
directed.representation_or_bridge: M turns ζ into the nearly constant product ζM; discretization is the bridge from an L2 statement at a random shift to a supremum over a continuum-sized short interval.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This is approximate inversion only on a high-probability event, for the stated σ0 and parameter choices. It does not assert that M is an exact reciprocal, nor that the same truncation is uniform for arbitrary interval growth.
directed.uncertainty: The prose and proof structure are recoverable, but X, νθ, σ0, and several exponent inequalities are formula-damaged and require scan verification.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Taking the logarithm of the finite Euler product changes a multiplicative inverse into the exponential of an additive prime-power field. The only mismatch with the factor-count-truncated mollifier is a high-Ω tail, which is made uniformly rare by exponential Rankin weighting and a mean-value bound.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The source defines a prime-power Dirichlet polynomial and writes its negative exponential as the finite product over p≤X of (1-p^{-s}). Expanding that product gives M(s) plus terms supported on integers composed of primes at most X with Ω(n)>νθ. Proposition 2.7 and the mean-value theorem bound the interval maximum in L2, while Rankin's trick inserts e^{Ω(n)-νθ}; the resulting Euler product is overwhelmed by the choice of νθ, and Markov gives a uniform o(1) probability.
directed.conceptual_reading: The useful compression is logarithmic: multiplicative cancellation against ζ becomes an additive field indexed by prime powers, which can later be split into scales. The high-factor tail measures exactly what this representation change forgets.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The finite Euler product is the bridge between the Möbius mollifier and exp(-P̃); Rankin weighting bridges a combinatorial factor-count cutoff to an analyzable Euler-product estimate.
directed.boundary_or_failure: M and exp(-P̃) are not identically equal because M excludes Ω(n)>νθ. Their closeness is probabilistic and uniform only in the specified off-axis interval and parameter regime.
directed.uncertainty: The identity and tail mechanism are clear, but fragmented displays obscure exact signs, prime-power indexing, and thresholds; these should be checked against the scan.

P_{K-2} is excluded to keep variances comparable, and P_0 is excluded so values at sufficiently separated h are nearly independent.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The moment lower bound is recast as an energy-entropy optimization: points at height γ log log T contribute an exponential βγ reward, while their available volume contributes Eθ(γ). Maximizing βγ+Eθ(γ) produces an interior quadratic regime until the optimizer reaches the maximum height, after which endpoint domination gives the linear frozen branch.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The proof defines a piecewise high-point exponent Eθ(γ), discretizes heights γ_j, and forms a good event asserting lower bounds for the volume of the corresponding level sets together with an upper bound on the field maximum. Restricting the exponential integral to a high-point set yields a lower bound by βγ_j plus Eθ(γ_j). Continuity turns the discrete maximum into max over γ, whose optimizer is interior below the critical β threshold and γ=m(θ) above it, giving the two branches of fθ(β).
directed.conceptual_reading: The phase transition is an optimizer collision, not a change in the integral's definition: increasing β shifts preference toward rarer high points until no admissible height remains above m(θ), so further gain comes only from reweighting the same extreme level.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Level-set volume bridges geometric information about high points to a lower bound on the exponential moment integral; the Legendre-type maximization bridges the entropy curve Eθ to the free-energy exponent.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The calculation is conditional on the good event and on later proof of the high-point volume bounds. It gives an exponent with ε losses, not a sharp finite-T identity.
directed.uncertainty: The optimization mechanism and regime split are clear, but the exact piecewise formula and critical threshold contain extraction-damaged fractions and should be scan-checked.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The second moment succeeds by matching probability cost to pair geometry. Most pairs are far enough apart to factorize and reproduce the square of the first moment; pairs sharing increments occupy progressively thinner distance bands, and the strict submaximum condition makes every correlated band's probability gain too small to offset its loss of volume.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The one-point estimate first gives E[N] at least (log T)^{Eθ(γ)-η/3}. Paley-Zygmund reduces the target to E[N^2]=(1+o(1))E[N]^2. Fubini expresses the second moment as a pair integral, partitioned into a far region B, a transition band, scale bands B_l, and a finest diagonal. Two-point factorization makes B the leading term. The correlated bound controls the other bands, and γ^2<m(θ)^2 supplies a negative exponent; the finest diagonal is bounded using the one-point probability.
directed.conceptual_reading: Correlation is not discarded but budgeted scale by scale. The proof works because the entropy of close pairs decreases faster than shared fluctuations make simultaneous exceedance more likely.
directed.representation_or_bridge: A distance-band partition turns the covariance hierarchy into a finite sum of exponent comparisons, allowing Paley-Zygmund to convert expected high-point volume into high-probability abundance.
directed.boundary_or_failure: Negligibility of correlated bands requires γ strictly below m(θ), η chosen small, and K then chosen sufficiently large. The argument does not cover the endpoint by the same second-moment estimate.
directed.uncertainty: The geometric mechanism and dependencies are explicit, while detailed log powers in the band estimates are formula-damaged and should be scan-checked.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The lower bound is assembled as an auditable sequence of representation changes: transfer ζ off axis, invert it with a mollifier, replace the mollifier by an exponential prime-power field, remove higher prime powers, trim endpoint prime blocks, and only then invoke the multiscale moment theorem. Each replacement has its own high-probability or negligible-error payment.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Proposition 3.6 first reduces the target critical-line moment to a slightly shorter off-axis ζ moment. Lemmas 3.7 and 3.9 use ζM≈1 and M≈exp(-P̃) to lower-bound it by an exponential integral of the prime-power field. Terms with prime-power exponent at least three are uniformly bounded, while the square-prime term is negligible with high probability by discretization and Lemma A.4. The remaining prime sum is decomposed into P_j, blocks j=0 and j=K-2 are discarded using earlier bounds, and Proposition 3.10 supplies the desired exponent.
directed.conceptual_reading: The proof is modular because each representation exposes the next controllable structure: analyticity enables line transfer, multiplicative inversion exposes an exponential, logarithms expose prime sums, and scale blocks expose branching correlations.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The chain is ζ moment → off-axis ζ → reciprocal mollifier → exp(prime powers) → exp(primes) → retained multiscale blocks. The explicit error and probability estimates certify each arrow rather than identifying the objects exactly.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The order cannot be freely rearranged, and the conclusion accumulates interval shrinkage and ε losses. All approximations hold on intersected high-probability events; none licenses deterministic equality of the representations.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Exact averaged moments of a real prime sum are encoded by a product of modified Bessel functions. Factoring that product into a quadratic exponential times a controlled analytic remainder isolates Gaussian variance, yields Gaussian even moments and usable tails, and remains valid after deleting early primes when their fourth-power remainder is small.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Lemma A.3 expresses kth moments of the symmetrized prime sum with |a(p)|≤1 through derivatives at zero of ∏_{p≤x} I0(|a(p)|z), plus an averaging error of order x^{2k}/T; odd moments are correspondingly small. For a(p)=p^{-σ-ih}, the product factors as F(z) times exp((z^2/4)Σp^{-2σ}), with controlled fixed derivatives of F. When x^{2k}/T=o(1), this gives Gaussian even moments for the real prime sum, also for y<p≤x, and a Gaussian-scale upper tail by choosing k from V^2/(2v^2).
directed.conceptual_reading: The Bessel product is a moment-generating surrogate for independent prime phases. Its quadratic part carries variance; the analytic remainder records non-Gaussian corrections that are negligible only within a bounded moment regime.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Averaged phase moments → Bessel Euler product → quadratic exponential → Gaussian moments and tail estimates. Removing small primes corresponds to zeroing coefficients and controlling the remaining fourth-power correction.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The Gaussian description is asymptotic and moment-limited: it requires x^{2k}/T=o(1), fixed-order remainder control, and V not too large. It is not a claim of exact Gaussianity or unrestricted independence of prime phases.
directed.uncertainty: The mechanism is explicit, but the Bessel normalization, moment factors, and admissible range are formula-heavy and need scan verification.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: When a sharp Gaussian asymptotic is unnecessary, a factorial 2l-moment bound turns coefficient energy into rapid exceptional-set control. Its flexibility comes from sacrificing sharp constants while retaining the decisive dependence l!(Σ|a(p)|²/p)^l.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Lemma A.4 bounds the averaged 2lth power of the prime Dirichlet polynomial Σ_{p≤x} a(p)p^{-1/2-iτ} by a constant times l! times (Σ_{p≤x}|a(p)|²/p)^l, for 2≤x≤T and natural l satisfying the stated restriction that x^l remain below the averaging scale T/log T.
directed.conceptual_reading: This is a robust energy-to-tail converter: coefficient L2 mass controls high moments, and Markov can trade the factorial growth against a chosen exceptional threshold without resolving the full distribution.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge is from a random-height Dirichlet polynomial to its weighted coefficient energy; factorial moments then feed union bounds, discretized maxima, and negligible-error estimates.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The estimate is crude and does not supply Gaussian asymptotics or covariance information. It must not be used outside the length-moment admissibility condition.
directed.uncertainty: The compact inequality is conceptually clear, but extraction obscures the exact comparison symbol in the admissibility condition and some normalization; scan verification is required.
